name: Batch vs Stream Processing
intent: Choose between computing results over a bounded pile of data on a schedule and computing them continuously as events arrive, trading freshness against completeness, cost and simplicity.
scenario: A shop wants orders per 10-minute window on a live dashboard and exact numbers for finance. One order happens at 10:09:55 but only reaches the pipeline at 10:11:30 because a phone was offline. The stream job has already published the 10:00 to 10:10 window; the nightly batch job will count the order correctly.
problem: Data is produced continuously but needs to be consumed at different speeds. A scheduled batch job over a bounded input is simple, cheap per record, easy to test and re-run, but its answers are as old as its schedule. A streaming job gives answers within seconds, but it must decide when a window is finished while events still arrive late and out of order (event time versus processing time), it holds state for as long as it runs, and a bug or a late event is much harder to repair. Picking the wrong one means either a dashboard that is hours behind or a streaming system nobody can reason about.

howItWorks.title: Batch: a bounded input, run to completion
howItWorks.text: A batch job reads a fixed set of data (yesterday's files or a table partition), processes all of it, writes the output and stops. Because the input is bounded and immutable, the job is deterministic: re-running it on the same input gives the same answer, so a bug is fixed by re-running. Throughput is the goal: big sequential reads, parallel workers, no state kept between runs. Typical latency is minutes to a day, set by the schedule plus the run time.

howItWorks.title: Stream: an unbounded input, run forever
howItWorks.text: A stream job reads an endless log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar), keeps small pieces of state in memory or a local store (counts per window, the latest value per key), and emits results continuously. Latency is milliseconds to seconds, but the job is a long-running service: it needs checkpoints, restarts without losing state, and capacity for the peak rate, 24 hours a day.

howItWorks.title: Event time versus processing time
howItWorks.text: Processing time is when the pipeline sees an event; event time is when it happened. They differ by network delay, retries and offline devices, from milliseconds to hours. A batch job simply waits until the day is over, so it sees nearly everything. A stream must decide when a window is complete without knowing if more events are on the way.

howItWorks.title: Watermarks: the stream's guess about completeness
howItWorks.text: A watermark is an estimate that no more events older than time T will arrive, often the newest event time seen minus a fixed allowed lateness. When it passes the end of a window the window is emitted. A short wait gives fresh answers but drops stragglers; a long wait is more complete but slower and holds more state. Events arriving after the window closed are dropped, sent to a side output, or trigger a corrected result (allowed lateness with updates).

howItWorks.title: Reconcile the two: reprocess, micro-batch, or unify
howItWorks.text: Lambda architecture runs both: a stream for a fast approximate view and a batch to overwrite it with the exact one, at the price of two code bases. Kappa architecture keeps one stream job and replays the retained log (days to weeks of Kafka retention) to reprocess. Micro-batching (Spark Structured Streaming, typically 1 to 10 second triggers) and engines like Flink or Beam that run the same logic on bounded and unbounded input narrow the gap. Whichever you pick, write results idempotently so replays and retries do not double count.

pros: Batch: simple mental model, deterministic and re-runnable, best throughput and cost per record, easy to test and backfill
Batch: sees (almost) all the data, so late events and corrections cost nothing extra
Stream: results within seconds, which enables alerts, fraud checks, live dashboards and reactive features
Stream: work is spread evenly over time instead of a nightly spike, and incremental state avoids re-reading history
cons: Batch: answers are as old as the schedule, and one big late failure delays everything downstream
Stream: you must reason about lateness, ordering, windows, state size and checkpoints; the failure modes are subtle
Stream: always on, so capacity is sized for peak and a stalled job is an incident, not a failed nightly run
Running both (Lambda) means two implementations that must agree, and they drift
whenToUse: Batch: reports, ML training sets, billing and finance numbers, big joins and backfills where a delay of hours is acceptable
Stream: the value of the answer decays in seconds or minutes: fraud detection, alerting, operational dashboards, personalisation
Micro-batch or hybrid: you need minutes of freshness but want batch-style simplicity and exactly-once sinks
whenNotToUse: Do not stream when nobody looks at the result more often than daily; a nightly job is cheaper and easier to fix
Do not batch when stale data causes real loss, such as approving a fraudulent payment an hour later
Do not run a Lambda setup if one engine can run the same logic on both bounded and unbounded input
Do not build a stream for small data: a cron job and a SQL query handle millions of rows a day without Kafka or Flink
pitfalls: Using processing time for windows, so a backlog or a replay puts yesterday's orders into today's windows
A watermark wait shorter than the real lateness distribution: the dashboard looks fine while 2 to 5% of events are silently dropped; measure and count late events
Treating a stream as exactly once without an idempotent or transactional sink, so a restart from the last checkpoint double counts
Unbounded state (a per-user window that never expires) until the job runs out of memory or the checkpoint takes minutes
Reprocessing a stream by replaying the log through the live job, which competes with real-time traffic and replays side effects such as emails
A single idle partition holds the watermark back, so windows never close even though other partitions are busy
Two code paths in Lambda that count slightly differently, so the dashboard jumps when the batch overwrites the stream

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: The service whose events (orders) are being counted.

roles.label: Event log
roles.description: A durable, replayable log such as Kafka that both jobs read from.

roles.label: Stream job
roles.description: A continuously running job that keeps window state and emits results when the watermark passes.

roles.label: Batch job
roles.description: A scheduled job that reads a bounded slice of the log and recomputes the result.

roles.label: Result table
roles.description: Where dashboards and finance read the counts; written idempotently by key.

quiz.question: A payments team scores card transactions for fraud once a night with a batch job. Fraudsters now drain accounts within minutes, and a flagged payment is only useful if it is blocked before it settles, a few seconds after it is made. Which change fits this need?
options: Move scoring to a stream job that decides on each payment as it arrives.
Run the same batch job every hour on a larger cluster, so results are at most an hour old.
Keep the nightly batch but make it faster, so the fraud list is ready by 6 a.m.
Switch to a daily micro-batch with a 24-hour trigger, so each batch is smaller.
quiz.explanation: The value of the answer decays in seconds, so only a continuous job meets it. Running the batch hourly, or finishing the nightly one sooner, is still far too slow, because fraud is paid out within minutes. A 24-hour trigger is the nightly job again.

quiz.question: A stream job counts orders per 10-minute window using the time the pipeline receives each event. The Kafka consumer is down for 2 hours, then restarts and works through the backlog at full speed. What does the dashboard show?
options: Correct counts for every window, because Kafka keeps the order of events and the job replays them.
Correct counts, but 2 hours late, because the watermark holds each window open until the backlog clears.
A spike after the restart and empty windows during the outage, because old orders are counted when processed.
The backlog is dropped as late data, so the outage windows stay empty and the later windows are accurate.
quiz.explanation: Windows based on processing time group events by when they were seen, not when they happened, so a backlog lands in the wrong windows. Windowing on event time with a watermark fixes this.

quiz.question: A stream job windows by event time and waits 10 seconds after the newest event before closing a window. About 4% of orders come from phones that were offline and arrive 1 to 5 minutes late. The dashboard looks smooth and finance later finds it undercounts. What is the best response?
options: Switch the windows to processing time, which never drops an event and so removes the problem.
Shorten the wait to 2 seconds so windows close faster and fewer late events are held in state.
Add more partitions to the topic, so the job reads faster and the late events are no longer late.
Measure how late events arrive, allow for that lateness or emit corrections, and count the drops.
quiz.explanation: A watermark shorter than the real lateness silently drops stragglers, so you tune it from measured data and watch the drops. Processing time avoids drops but puts events in the wrong windows, and more partitions do not change when a phone sends its data.
